title: C++ Exception Handling: Quick Revision
summary: Night-before revision notes on C++ exceptions: throw/try/catch, the standard hierarchy, noexcept, exception safety guarantees, RAII and stack unwinding, error codes versus exceptions, and std::expected.

chapters.title: Exceptions: The Mental Model
points: throw transfers control up the call stack to the nearest matching catch; the current function stops immediately and no normal return happens
try { ... } catch (const T& e) { ... } is the handler form; handlers are tried top to bottom and the first match wins, so list derived types before bases
catch (...) catches anything, including non-std types; use it last, and rethrow with a bare `throw;` to keep the original exception object
Throw by value, catch by const reference: `throw std::runtime_error("x"); catch (const std::exception& e)`. This avoids slicing and extra copies
An uncaught exception calls std::terminate, which aborts the program; main() with no handler still terminates without guaranteed full unwinding

chapters.title: Standard Exception Hierarchy and Custom Types
points: std::exception is the root and has a virtual `what()` returning const char*; its subclasses are logic_error and runtime_error
logic_error branch: invalid_argument, out_of_range, length_error, domain_error. These flag preventable programmer or contract bugs
runtime_error branch: range_error, overflow_error, underflow_error, system_error. These flag failures found only at runtime
Other library throws: bad_alloc from new, bad_cast from dynamic_cast on references, bad_optional_access, bad_variant_access, and out_of_range from vector::at()
Custom exception: `struct DbError : std::runtime_error { using std::runtime_error::runtime_error; };`. Derive from std::exception so one catch handles it
Catching by value slices the derived object and loses its type and what() text; catch by const& instead. Catching by pointer is also wrong

chapters.title: noexcept and Exception Safety Guarantees
points: noexcept promises a function never lets an exception escape; if one does, std::terminate runs, with no unwinding guarantee. `noexcept(expr)` is the conditional form and `noexcept(f())` is the query operator
Destructors are implicitly noexcept; throwing from one during unwinding terminates the program, so catch inside destructors
Move constructors and move assignment should be noexcept: std::vector reallocation uses move_if_noexcept, so a throwing move falls back to slow copying

Four guarantees, weakest to strongest: no guarantee (leaks or corrupt state), basic (invariants hold, no leaks, state valid but unspecified), strong (commit or rollback, state unchanged on failure), nothrow (never fails; swap and destructors)
Strong guarantee idiom is copy-and-swap: do all throwing work on a temp copy, then commit with a noexcept swap

chapters.title: RAII and Stack Unwinding
points: RAII: acquire the resource in a constructor and release it in the destructor, so the resource lifetime equals the object lifetime
Stack unwinding: when an exception propagates, every fully constructed local in each exited scope is destroyed in reverse order of construction, running destructors
If a constructor throws, the object's destructor does not run; already-constructed members and bases are destroyed. Raw `new` followed by a throw leaks, which is why members should themselves be RAII
Standard RAII types: unique_ptr and make_unique, shared_ptr, lock_guard and scoped_lock, fstream, vector and string. Prefer them over manual new/delete or lock()/unlock()
Raw `new`, `fopen` or `lock()` with a later cleanup call leaks when an exception skips the cleanup line; wrap the resource in an object. Never throw from a destructor

chapters.title: Error Codes vs Exceptions vs std::expected
points: Use exceptions for rare, exceptional failures that the caller cannot handle locally, such as a constructor failing or an allocation failure; they can't be silently ignored, and the happy path has zero cost

Use error codes or return values for expected, frequent failures such as parse or lookup misses, in hot paths, and in no-exception builds (-fno-exceptions). The catch is that callers can ignore them, so mark them [[nodiscard]]
Cost model: a throw is slow, roughly microseconds, because of unwinding and RTTI lookup; a non-throwing path adds no runtime cost on mainstream ABIs
C++23 `std::expected<T,E>` holds either a value or an error: `return std::unexpected(Err::NotFound);` The caller checks `if (r)`, then `*r` or `r.value()`, and `r.error()` for the error

expected monadic chain: `.and_then(f)`, `.transform(f)`, `.or_else(f)` compose steps without nested ifs. `value()` throws bad_expected_access<E> if there is an error, and `value_or(x)` gives a default
Common mistakes: using exceptions for ordinary control flow, mixing styles without a boundary (convert at API edges), and dereferencing an expected without checking it

chapters.title: Exception Handling Cheat Sheet
points: Syntax: `throw X(...)`; `catch (const X& e)`; `catch (...)`; rethrow with `throw;` (never `throw e;`, which copies and slices)
Hierarchy: std::exception → logic_error (invalid_argument, out_of_range) and runtime_error (overflow_error, system_error); also bad_alloc, bad_cast
noexcept rules: destructors and moves are noexcept; a throw out of noexcept means terminate; swap is nothrow
Guarantees: basic, strong (copy-and-swap), nothrow. Use RAII for everything: unique_ptr, lock_guard, fstream
Decision: exceptions for rare, unrecoverable-locally failures; expected or error codes for frequent, expected failures; [[nodiscard]] on error returns
